paragraphs.en: Typoholism is a game where you can practise your typing speed, accuracy and memory. You can play on your own, compete with friends or simply track your progress.

There are several modes to choose from, ranging from leisurely story transcription to challenges where every second counts. This guide explains how to start a game, how each mode works and what to pay attention to while typing.

Your goal is to type as quickly as possible while making as few mistakes as you can. Depending on the mode, you'll transcribe a prepared text, type random words, remember increasingly long word sequences or race against the clock.
You can play alone or with up to seven other people. In multiplayer, players compete for the best score, with victory depending on both the average number of correctly typed words per minute and accuracy, measured by the number of mistakes made.
The main mode is Free Typing, where everyone transcribes the same text. Speed matters, but mistakes reduce your final score, so a more accurate player can win even if they type a little more slowly.
The other modes let you practise different skills. Random Words tests your typing skills, Memory Chain challenges you to remember words in order, and Survival puts your reactions to the test.
Start by creating a game table. You can set it up for solo practice or invite other players to join you.
Your most important choice is the game mode. Each of the four modes offers a different kind of challenge and lets you tailor the game to your preferences.

Free Typing involves transcribing a selected text. You can use the built-in stories, your own files or pasted text. You can also set a time limit or, when playing solo, dispense with the source text and write something of your own.
Random Words challenges you to type words presented by the game one at a time. You can use a regular keyboard, Braille input or a mixed mode that changes the input method from word to word.
Memory Chain tests how well you can remember a growing sequence of words. With each attempt, you must reproduce all the words presented so far in the correct order.
Survival combines typing random words with a race against the clock. You choose a difficulty level that determines the starting pace.
Once you've configured the table, you can begin practising or publish it so that others can join. Standard PowerGames features are available, including invitations, spectating, chat and game history.
You'll find the detailed rules for each mode and its available settings in the Game modes and table options section.
At the start of each new round, focus automatically returns to the typing field. If you move to another part of the interface during play, return focus to that field to continue.
The game reads out the words you need to type. Depending on the mode, it may also read entire sentences or ask you to recall words you heard earlier.
Usually, you confirm a word by pressing Space after typing it. The exception is Survival, where a correctly completed word is confirmed automatically.

Mistakes are handled differently depending on the mode. In Free Typing, you can correct the current word with Backspace until you confirm it with Space. In the other modes, the game checks each character as you type. If you press an incorrect key, it waits for the correct one instead of moving on.
During play, you can have words read aloud (Ctrl+O) or spelled out (Ctrl+L), and use other shortcuts to repeat parts of the text. Check the shortcuts list to discover all the available commands.

When transcribing texts, you don't have to match letter case or reproduce every decorative typographic character. The game accepts simpler keyboard equivalents for all types of quotation marks, spaces, dashes and ellipses.
If the text contains numbers, the game will tell you to enter them as digits.
When you import your own text, you'll also be notified of any unsupported characters that need changing.
How a game ends depends on the selected mode.
In Free Typing, a round ends when you finish transcribing the text, the set time limit expires, or you choose End Typing.
In Random Words, Memory Chain and Survival, a round ends after five mistakes. You can also end it manually.
In multiplayer, the results appear once everyone has finished. The player with the highest score wins. If two or more players have exactly the same score, it's a tie.
In a match consisting of multiple rounds, the overall winner is determined by the number of rounds won.
Typoholism rewards both typing proficiency and accuracy. That's why your final score isn't simply the number of words you typed.

In Free Typing, one measure of performance is WPM, or correctly typed words per minute. The game counts the time spent typing them, but not the time spent listening before you press the first key of a word. You can therefore listen to the whole word first to make sure you know what to type.
In Random Words, Memory Chain and Survival, the score is based on the number of correctly typed words.
In every mode, the game also calculates an accuracy factor. This is the number of correct words divided by the total of correct words and mistakes.
The base score is then multiplied by that accuracy factor twice.
For example, if you type 20 words correctly and make 4 mistakes, your final score will be approximately 13.89 points.

Someone who types 17 words without a single mistake will score 17 points and win.
As you can see, typing as fast as possible isn't always the best strategy. A slightly slower but more accurate approach can pay off.
The summary displays your final score and accuracy percentage.
Each Typoholism mode has slightly different rules. The differences involve not only the task itself, but also how mistakes are corrected, how words are confirmed and which settings are available.
In this mode, you transcribe a selected text word by word, either using regular typing or by simulating a Braille keyboard layout. In multiplayer, everyone receives the same text.
At the beginning, the game reads the current sentence, followed by the first word you need to type.
Type it exactly, including punctuation, and press Space to continue.
Until you confirm a word, you can correct it with Backspace. Once you press Space, the game checks the word and moves on to the next one.

If you make a mistake, you'll hear a distinctive sound and a message, but the game will continue.
You can choose from built-in texts in the table settings, import your own files or paste any text.
Once you select a text, its title and character count, including spaces, appear in the table description. They are also displayed in the table widget, allowing other players to estimate the length of the game before joining.
To use your own material, choose Paste Text. Enter its title in the table settings, then press Tab to move to the text field.

Imported files must use UTF-8 encoding. The maximum size of a file or pasted text is 1,000 kB. Since some characters take up more than one byte, this corresponds to slightly fewer than a million characters. Your texts are stored locally on your computer. However, if you use your own text in multiplayer, it is shared with the participants through the Elten server when the game starts.
By default, Free Typing continues until the entire text is finished. If you'd prefer a shorter game, you can set a time limit. When it expires, the round ends even if you're in the middle of a word.
When playing solo, you can also choose to type without a source text. Instead of transcribing something prepared, you write your own text. Without a time limit, you can keep writing for as long as you like. To finish such a session, choose End Typing.
When transcribing a built-in text on your own, the game saves your progress locally when you finish or leave. This lets you resume later rather than starting the same text again. If you want to repeat it from the beginning, reset its progress in Local Texts and Progress.
In this mode, the game reads out randomly selected words one after another. Your task is to type each one correctly and confirm it with Space.

Unlike Free Typing, each character is checked as soon as you enter it. If you press the wrong key, you make one mistake, but the cursor stays in place. You must enter the correct character to continue.
Backspace doesn't work because incorrect characters aren't added to the correctly typed beginning of the word.

Multiplayer games also have a five-second inactivity limit.
If you don't start typing or continue typing within that time, you receive a mistake. The timer also runs before you press the first key.
You can use the appropriate shortcut to have the word read aloud or spelled out. The timer pauses while the screen reader is speaking, and once it finishes, you get a full five seconds again.

There is no inactivity penalty when playing solo, so you can practise at your own pace.
In this mode's settings, you can choose a regular keyboard, Braille input or mixed mode.
In mixed mode, the game randomly selects an input method for each word.
You'll find more information about Braille input later in this guide.
This mode is about remembering an increasingly long sequence of words.
First, the game gives you one word to type. It then adds another, but reads aloud only the new word.
Each time, you must reproduce the entire sequence from the beginning, separating the words with Space.
For example, if you first hear “cat” and then “garden”, you must type both words in the correct order. When a third word is added, you type all three.
Each attempt gets harder as there are more words to remember.
As in Random Words, an incorrect character adds one mistake but doesn't move the cursor, and Backspace isn't available. This mode also has the same inactivity penalty and supports Braille input.
Mixed mode here is for incurable nerds, because you have to recall both the word and the way you were supposed to type it.
In Survival, you need to type each new word before the music stops playing.
Each word has its own time limit, determined by the length of the recording.
You can choose one of three difficulty levels in the table settings.

- Easy - approximately 16 seconds at the start.
- Medium - approximately 10.67 seconds at the start.
- Hard - approximately 6.64 seconds at the start.
After every correctly completed word, the music speeds up by 2.5 percent and its pitch rises.

This means that the longer you play without mistakes, the less time you have to type each new word.
In this mode, you don't confirm words with Space. As soon as you type the last correct character, the game moves to the next word automatically.
If you press the wrong key, you get a mistake but keep the correctly typed beginning of the word.

If the music ends before you've finished a word, the game adds a mistake and starts a new word. In that case, the music doesn't speed up.
Remember that reading words aloud, spelling them out and muting the music do not stop the countdown.
There is no separate inactivity timer here, because the music itself sets the time limit for each word.
You can also use a regular keyboard, Braille input or mixed mode here.
Instead of entering characters with individual keys, you can use a layout that simulates a Braille keyboard.
Braille dots correspond to the following keys.

- Dots 1, 2 and 3 - F, D, S.
- Dots 4, 5 and 6 - J, K, L.
- Dot 7 - A.
- Dot 8 - semicolon.

To enter a Braille character, press the corresponding keys together, then release them.
In Typoholism Settings, you can choose different Braille tables for your language, or a local Liblouis table provided as a ctb, utb, tbl or uti file.
Press Ctrl+P to open Typoholism Settings.
Here you can configure Braille input, typing echo, error notifications and music volume.
Typing echo controls what the game reads aloud as you type.
You can follow Elten's settings, have characters read aloud, have words read aloud, hear both characters and words, or turn echo off entirely.

These changes apply only to the typing field during the game.
Another setting controls how the game informs you about mistakes.

Spoken and sound notifications are independent. You can enable both, choose just one or turn notifications off completely.
The final option is a music volume slider ranging from 0 to 100 percent.
In Random Words, Memory Chain and Survival, you can choose a fixed number of rounds or play a match that continues until the host ends it.
In each round, players earn scores according to the rules of the selected mode.
In a multi-round match, the overall winner is the player who wins the most rounds.
This allows for both a quick game and a longer tournament in which a single setback doesn't necessarily decide the final result.

Touch typing means entering text without looking at the keyboard. With regular practice, you'll learn to find keys automatically, which can improve your typing speed, accuracy, and comfort. Touch typing is a valuable skill for people in many professions where typing speed directly affects productivity, such as programmers, journalists, and writers.
Place the fingers of your left hand on the A, S, D, and F keys, and those of your right hand on J, K, L, and the semicolon (;). Rest your thumbs on the spacebar.
The F and J keys have small raised bumps that help you find the starting position for both hands without looking.

This is your home position. From here, you can type other characters by moving your fingers to nearby keys. For example, to type z, move your left pinky down from a. To type q, move the same finger up. To type y, move your right index finger diagonally up and to the left from j.

title.en: Five Golden Rules of Touch Typing

paragraphs.en: 1. Use all your fingers. Each finger is assigned specific keys. Try to follow these assignments while learning.
2. Return to the home position. After pressing a key, move your finger back to its starting position. For example, after typing r, return your left index finger to f.
3. Use your thumb for the spacebar. For capital letters, use the Shift key on the opposite side of the keyboard. For example, use the right Shift key to type A, and the left Shift key to type K.
4. Keep your hands relaxed. Make light, natural movements and keep your wrists as straight as comfortably possible.
5. Don't rush. Focus on accuracy first. Speed will come with practice.
Practice regularly. Start with short sessions lasting around 10-15 minutes.
Focus on accuracy. Try to minimize typing errors before gradually increasing your speed.
Repeat difficult combinations. If a particular key or word gives you trouble, spend some extra time practicing it.
Track your progress. Compare your results across training sessions, but remember that speed isn't everything.
Take breaks. If you start losing concentration or feel discomfort in your hands, stop practicing and rest.
- Ctrl+L: Spell the current word.
- Ctrl+O: Read the current word.
- Ctrl+;: Read the rest of the word (unavailable in Memory Chain).
- Ctrl+Shift+;: Read the rest of the sentence (Free Typing).
- Alt+S: Read progress.
- Ctrl+P: Open typing settings.
- Space: Confirm the word (except Survival).
- Backspace: Correct the current word (Free Typing).
- Ctrl+S: Save and close the table.
- F1: Contextual help.
- Ctrl+F1: Game help.
- Escape: Leave the table.
